Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a connected closed Riemann surface, let $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_m$, $m\ge1$, be disjoint smooth embedded circles, and put $L=q(\gamma_1\times\cdots\times\gamma_m)\subset\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$. Let $u:\overline{\mathbb D}\to\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ be smooth, holomorphic in the interior for the standard complex structure, with boundary on $L$. For a component $R$ of $\Sigma\setminus\bigcup_i\gamma_i$, let $n_R(u)$ be its actual relative divisor-intersection degree, evaluated at any point of $R$.

If $u$ is nonconstant and $n_R(u)\in\{0,1\}$ for every $R$, then the set
$$I(u)=\{z\in\mathbb D:du(z)\ne0,\ u^{-1}(u(z))=\{z\}\text{ in }\overline{\mathbb D}\}$$
is open and dense in $\mathbb D$. In particular this applies to every nonconstant integrable disk whose actual domain is one cut component with coefficient one and zero on the others.

This is an integrable zero-one-domain statement. It neither factors arbitrary disks nor asserts that all index-two disks have such domains, that a perturbed almost complex disk automatically has dense injective points, or that the resulting moduli space is regular or has a specified count.

Let $S$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with smooth boundary and a supplied finite smooth triangulation. This means finite face-to-face triangular disks with circular interior vertex links and interval boundary vertex links; each face has an orientation-preserving parametrization by a closed Euclidean triangle whose derivative is nonsingular and smooth on a neighborhood of that triangle in a surface chart. Let $v$ be a supplied smooth tangent field on $S$, with finitely many isolated interior zeros, none on the triangulation's vertices or edges. Suppose $v$ is a positive multiple of the positively oriented tangent along every boundary component. The boundary may be empty.

At each zero $p$, define $\operatorname{ind}_p(v)$ as the winding of the nonzero coordinate vector $v$ along a sufficiently small positively oriented coordinate circle around $p$. This integer is independent of the positively oriented coordinate and of the small circle. Then, with $V,E,F$ the given finite triangulation counts,
$$\sum_{p:v(p)=0}\operatorname{ind}_p(v)=V-E+F=\chi(S).$$
There is no choice assumption. The assertion is conditional on the supplied smooth triangulation and field; it does not claim a triangulation or generic field exists in a more general category.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed Riemann surface and $m\ge1$. Give $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ its usual complex charts of elementary symmetric coordinates in disjoint support disks. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to X$ be the quotient and $p_i:\Sigma^m\to\Sigma$ its factor projections. For $i<j$ let $\Delta_{ij}=\{z_i=z_j\}$, and put $R=\sum_{i<j}\Delta_{ij}$, with coefficient one on every pair diagonal, including at their intersections. Then there is a holomorphic line-bundle isomorphism
$$q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\cong\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^m p_i^*T\Sigma\right)\otimes\mathcal O(R).$$
Under this isomorphism the holomorphic section $\det(dq)$ of
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}\left(\bigotimes_i p_i^*T\Sigma,q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\right)$$
corresponds to the canonical divisor section of $\mathcal O(R)$. In particular its zero divisor is exactly $R$, even at tuples with three or more equal entries; no transverse-intersection or simple-branch hypothesis is needed for the bundle identity.

Here $\mathcal O(R)$ is constructed by the actual local defining functions in the proof. For a smooth map $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):C\to\Sigma^m$ from a closed oriented surface with supplied finite smooth triangle data, the identity implies the degree formula
$$\deg\bigl((qF)^*\det(TX)\bigr)=\sum_i\deg(f_i^*T\Sigma)+\sum_{i<j}\deg\bigl((f_i,f_j)^*\mathcal O(\Delta)\bigr),$$
where $\Delta\subset\Sigma\times\Sigma$ is the ordinary diagonal. Degree means the finite face-winding degree of a complex line bundle. Whenever a pulled-back diagonal section has finitely many isolated zeros, its degree is the sum of their signed local winding indices; at a transverse coincidence this is the sign of $d(f_i-f_j)$ in an oriented surface coordinate. Degrees remain defined if two maps coincide identically.

For $m=1$ the empty divisor has its trivial line and constant section one; $q$ is the identity. For $m=0$ all determinants and tensor products over the one-point symmetric product are trivial and the degree formula is zero. This result does not identify the diagonal class in surface cohomology, compute a sphere's degree, prove a Maslov/domain formula, or realize arbitrary Whitney classes by incidence covers.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E\to\overline{\mathbb D}$ be a smooth complex vector bundle of rank $m\ge1$, with complex multiplication $J$, and let $F\subset E|_{\partial\mathbb D}$ be a smooth oriented totally real real subbundle of rank $m$. Let $P$ be a smooth real-linear first-order operator on sections with exact Cauchy–Riemann symbol: for real smooth $h$ and smooth $\xi$,
$$P(h\xi)=hP\xi+h_x\xi+h_yJ\xi.$$
Use smooth positive definite metrics and finite smooth charts to define $H^r(E)$ by weak derivatives for integers $r\ge1$. Let $X_0$ be the $H^1$ closure of smooth sections with boundary values in $F$, and put $X_q=H^{q+1}(E)\cap X_0$, $Y_q=H^q(E)$ for integers $q\ge0$. Only the zeroth boundary condition is imposed.

There is a smooth global complex frame of $E$ and an integer $k$ in which the boundary condition is
$$F(e^{it})=e^{ikt}\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R^{m-1}$$
and the actual operator is $\partial_x+i\partial_y+B$ with smooth real-linear zeroth-order coefficient $B$. Equivalently, before this reduction, if $C(t)$ is the complex matrix whose columns are any smooth periodic oriented real frame of $F$ in any global complex frame, then
$$k=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{(\det C)'(t)}{\det C(t)}\,dt.$$
Such frames exist, and this integer is independent of both choices.

Every actual realization $P_q:X_q\to Y_q$ is bounded Fredholm with real index $m+2k$. Its kernel is the same set as the $H^1$ kernel, its range is $Y_q\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0$, and inclusion in $L^2$ identifies its real cokernel with that of $P_0$. For $\xi\in X_0$ and $P\xi=f\in H^q$,
$$\|\xi\|_{H^{q+1}}\le C_q(\|f\|_{H^q}+\|\xi\|_{H^1}).$$
The inverse of $P_0$ from its $H^1$ kernel complement to its closed range is bounded, and its restriction gives a bounded range inverse $H^q\cap\operatorname{Ran}P_0\to X_q$. The statement applies to an actual geometric linearization along a smooth disk with oriented totally real boundary. It does not assert its surjectivity, compute a Heegaard domain formula, or supply a puncture or gluing theorem.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X$ have real dimension $2m$, $m\ge1$, and be the compact target in the actual boundary-preserving local-addition theorem, let $L$ be one of its oriented product tori, and let $x$ be a generator. Let $J$ be a smooth autonomous almost complex structure for which $L$ is totally real. Near $x$ require one fixed chart taking $J$ to $i$, $L$ to $\mathbb R^m$ and $x$ to zero. Fix a boundary point $p$ of the disk.

There is an actual second-countable Hilbert manifold, constructed as the union of local-addition charts at smooth boundary-compatible node-fixed references, of $H^3$ disk maps with boundary in $L$ and value $x$ at $p$. It contains all smooth such maps; no approximation assertion for every arbitrary constrained rough map is required. Near a smooth reference map its model is the space of $H^3$ sections with the zeroth $TL$ boundary trace and $\xi(p)=0$, intersected with the actual $H^1$ completed boundary domain, not an asserted higher-norm smooth closure. The Cauchy–Riemann expression is an actual smooth $H^2$ section; its zeros are smooth maps. If the boundary determinant winding of the full disk problem is $k$, its actual full linearization has real index $m+2k$, and its node-fixed realization has index $2k$. Write $\mu=2k$ for this actual node-fixed operator index.

At a smooth zero, compact node-fixed surjectivity is equivalent to surjectivity of the actual weighted node-fixed punctured-disk realization, for every integer order and each weight $0<\delta<\pi$. No surjectivity is assumed without this explicit operator condition. At a nonconstant zero satisfying it, the actual node-fixed zero space is locally a smooth $\mu$-dimensional manifold. The explicit positive affine group $z\mapsto az+b$, $a>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, of holomorphic half-plane automorphisms fixing infinity acts freely and properly, and smoothly on this regular zero manifold. Its quotient has local smooth slices of dimension $\mu-2$. In particular when $\mu=2$ every regular such disk is locally isolated modulo these automorphisms. No global count or compactness is concluded.

Finally if $u=v\circ\psi$ for a smooth degree-$d$ disk map $\psi$ taking boundary to boundary and the marked point to the marked point, then $\mu(u)=d\mu(v)$ for the corresponding actual Cauchy–Riemann-symbol indices. In particular a disk of actual node-fixed index two cannot be a nontrivial proper holomorphic disk cover of degree $d>1$: the oriented torus makes $\mu(v)$ even. This does not assert that every nonsimple disk admits such a covering factorization, or prove generic regularity, boundary-degeneration classification, gluing or cancellation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $K\subseteq M$ be compact, and let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $K\subseteq W$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:M\to [0,1]$ that equals $1$ on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq W$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and write $f=u+iv:U\to\mathbb C$. Suppose the four first partial derivatives of $u$ and $v$ exist on a neighbourhood of $a$, are continuous at $a$, and satisfy

$$ u_x(a)=v_y(a),\qquad u_y(a)=-v_x(a). $$

Then $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$. Consequently, if these hypotheses hold at every point of $U$, then $f$ is holomorphic on $U$.

Let $f$ be holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $a$. A holomorphic function has finite order $m$ at $a$ if and only if, on some neighbourhood of $a$, it has the form $f(z)=(z-a)^m g(z)$ with $g$ holomorphic and $g(a)\ne0$.

Moreover, $\operatorname{ord}_a(f)=+\infty$ if and only if $f$ vanishes on a neighbourhood of $a$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, let $F:U\to\mathbb C^m$ be
holomorphic, and let $a\in U$. If $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)\ne0$, then there are
open neighbourhoods $U_0\subseteq U$ of $a$ and $V_0$ of $F(a)$ such that
$F|_{U_0}:U_0\to V_0$ is biholomorphic.

If $G:V_0\to U_0$ denotes the inverse, then

$$DG(w)=DF(G(w))^{-1}\qquad(w\in V_0).$$

derivations.claim: Use [F1]'s actual incidence cover. Every point of the open cut component belonging to $A$ has exactly one active interior inverse point, by its exact unit-degree identity; no point in another cut region has one. Each active component has an open image meeting $A$, and different active interior images are disjoint. Since $A$ is connected, there is exactly one active component $S$. Every other root component is constant at some $c_j\in\gamma_j$. At the physical boundary each circle label selects exactly one root of the tuple. Thus the incidence cover is unbranched there, each boundary circle has one label and maps with degree one to the physical source circle, and there is exactly one incidence boundary circle per label. A constant component therefore has covering degree one and is a constant root disk. In particular $p|_S$ has degree equal to the number of active boundary labels. The finite exceptional root set from [F1] contains all interior ramification of this map. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

We justify the complete boundary alternatives. Near every point of $\partial S$, extend a real analytic regular parametrization of its labelled $\gamma_j$ by its convergent complex power series. Its derivative is nonzero, so [F6] gives a holomorphic inverse coordinate taking that circle arc to the real line. By [F6] the nonconstant root extends across the source boundary. It has local form a nonzero real multiple of $z^b$ after real-preserving local coordinates. Interior injectivity forces $b\le2$: a power of order at least three maps two different points of the open half-disk to the same point. The case $b=2$ is a simple slit tip; its open half-disk maps onto a punctured neighborhood minus one ray. The case $b=1$ is one regular bank. There are finitely many tips, since the extended derivative zeros are isolated and the boundary is compact. An interior root preimage of a boundary image is impossible: its open image is a full neighborhood, while that boundary preimage also supplies a nonempty open half-neighborhood, duplicating nearby points outside the circles, contrary to [F1]. Hence interior and boundary images are disjoint. [F1, F6, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Choose a smooth field $V$ on $\Sigma$, tangent and nonzero on every $\gamma_j$, with finitely many isolated zeros and no zero at any of the finitely many root collision values. Start with a nonzero oriented tangent in signed circle collars, extend it by finite bumps, and perturb only on the compact complement using [F5]. A finite set can be avoided by prescribing a nonzero local value there before the perturbation. The zeros are then finite and transverse; move the supplied finite face edges away from them. On each cut component its zero-index sum equals its Euler characteristic by [F2]. To meet that supplier's POSITIVE boundary convention, if the chosen field points in the opposite boundary direction multiply it on that component by $e^{i\theta}$, where $\theta$ is zero or $\pi$ near the respective boundary circles and is extended across the component by finitely many collar bumps. This introduces no zero or index change and makes it positive on all boundaries. Hence the original field's zero indices in $A$ sum to $\chi(A)$. Its pullback along the active interior has one inverse point for every such zero, preserving its local index by [F1]'s orientation-positive local inverse. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

If only one side of $\gamma_j$ belongs to $A$, every point of that circle is a boundary image: approach it from $A$, use compactness of $S$, and exclude an interior limit because it would cover the other side too. A tip would likewise cover both sides, so no tip occurs. Its active boundary circle is a local diffeomorphism onto the whole $\gamma_j$, with degree one by injectivity of interior banks. Thus each of the $e$ external copies supplies one full active boundary. If both sides belong to $A$ and its root is constant, no active boundary has that label; the same compactness argument makes every point of that circle an active INTERIOR image. If its root is active, let $K_j$ be its connected compact boundary image. At a regular point of $K_j$ both adjacent sides of $A$ must be covered, so there are exactly two boundary banks, one from each side. A tip value has only its one tip preimage: that tip already covers a punctured neighborhood except its slit ray, and any other preimage would duplicate an open set. Compactness of the remainder of the boundary then gives a neighborhood of that value in which only its tip neighborhood contributes; along $\gamma_j$ this image is one-sided. Therefore each tip is an endpoint of $K_j$. There must be a tip: without one a connected boundary circle maps as an unbranched circle covering of fixed orientation, whereas the required two banks have opposite orientations. The image cannot be the whole target circle, since it has this one-sided endpoint neighborhood. It is therefore one proper closed arc, with exactly two endpoints and their order-two tips, and exactly two regular banks elsewhere. Finally a circle neither of whose sides belongs to $A$ has a constant root, since a nonconstant boundary bank would cover an adjacent open region. This proves all the asserted alternatives. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Let $a$ count the internal circles of the slit type. The active interior image consists exactly of $A$ with each internal pair filled and with those $a$ slit arcs removed. Indeed every point off the circle system was accounted for by [F1]; on an internal circle, a point outside its boundary image has an interior inverse point by compactness, while step2.1 excludes such a point on the boundary image. The compact source is its normalization with the two banks separated, by the regular-bank and quadratic-tip models of step2.1. Glue each internal pair of boundary circles of the planar $A$. This leaves Euler characteristic unchanged, since a circle has Euler characteristic zero. At each slit remove a small open regular-neighborhood disk about that embedded interior arc; its boundary contracts to the two banks and two quadratic tips. This is exactly the same compact surface normalization up to a collar change, so it decreases Euler characteristic by one. Consequently $\chi(S)=\chi(A)-a$, and step3.1 gives $r=e+a$. Counting finite cells of the degree-$r$ branched cover gives $\chi(S)=r-R_p$: triangulate its base disk with its finitely many branch values as vertices; edges and faces have $r$ lifts, while a point of local degree $b$ loses $b-1$ of the usual lifted vertex count. The boundary is unbranched. Thus $R_p=r-\chi(S)$. The constant roots met by the active interior are exactly those on the $\ell-a$ filled internal circles; each is met once, and roots on all other constant labels lie outside this image. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Off root collisions define a section $s$ of $(u^*\det TX)^{\otimes2}$ by taking the square of the wedge of $dq(V(z_1)),\ldots,dq(V(z_m))$. Permuting roots changes the wedge by a real sign only, so its square is well defined. By [F3] its local expression is a nonzero constant times the squared Vandermonde times $\prod_i V(z_i)^2$ in target tangent coordinates. It extends continuously by zero at collisions. At a zero of $V$ away from collisions its index is twice that field index, with multiplicities added if several roots have zeros at the same base point; step2.2 excludes zeros at collision values. At a branch of the active base map $p$ of local degree $b$, the active root map is a local coordinate by [F1]. The $b$ active roots are the $b$ roots of the base parameter up to a holomorphic coordinate change. Their squared Vandermonde has winding $b-1$, as the product of pair differences is a unit times its elementary power-model product. Thus the total contribution of such branches is $R_p$. Each collision of one constant root with the active root contributes an additional $2$: in the active root coordinate $w$, the product of its differences from that constant value over the local $p$-sheets is a unit times the base parameter, so its SQUARE has winding two, including when that point is also a branch of $p$. Distinct constant roots cannot coincide, since their labels are disjoint circles. Active roots have no other collisions except branches, by [F1]. These cases exhaust the zeros of $s$. The extension and index calculations use continuous nonzero unit factors, so no false smoothness assertion about a general smooth field in symmetric root coordinates is required. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

Along the physical boundary the tuple has distinct entries and every $V(z_i)$ is a nonzero tangent vector to its labelled circle. Their wedge is therefore a real basis determinant for $TL$ in the actual complex target frame; its square is the squared determinant boundary phase times a positive scalar. Trivialize $u^*TX$ over the disk by finite disk frames. The winding of this nonzero boundary section is exactly its Maslov index. Finite zero excision for the continuous section $s$ identifies it with the sum of the indices from step5.1. Consequently $$\mu(u)=2\chi(A)+R_p+2(\ell-a).$$ Since $A$ is planar with $e+2\ell$ boundary copies, $\chi(A)=2-e-2\ell$. Substitute step4.1's $R_p=e+a-(\chi(A)-a)$ to obtain $\mu(u)=\chi(A)+e+2\ell=2$. All signs come from the actual positive complex local coordinates and squared determinant section, not a presumed index-domain formula. [F2, F3, F4, step 4.1, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]

The compact operator result [F4] now gives real Fredholm index $m+2$ on all its stated higher integer Sobolev realizations. On the $H^3\to H^2$ realization the point trace is bounded by [F4], and evaluation at a boundary point is onto on the full domain: in a small boundary chart multiply any chosen vector in $T_xL$ by a scalar bump equal to one there, and extend by zero. Its codimension-$m$ kernel is the fixed-node domain. Restricting a Fredholm operator to a closed finite-codimension domain lowers its index by that codimension; its range is closed, as follows by projecting to a complement of the finite-dimensional operator kernel. Thus the node-fixed index is two. This does not assert that node evaluation is onto on the operator kernel or that either operator is onto. The proof includes a possible singly pointed domain with all region coefficients one if a disk actually exists; it makes no existence or count claim. It retains all slit and filled-circle cases needed in the multipointed setting. [F4, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎

boundaries.reason: Statement assumes a nonconstant disk and an actual nonempty cut component.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 permits a=0 or e=0 and no source ramification if the actual disk data allow it.
Step 1.1 treats exactly one active component, m=1 and constant other root components with boundary degree one.
Steps 2.1 through 4.1 include filled internal circles, two-bank slit arcs, order-two tips and possible node/branch coincidences; no generic boundary map imposed.
Steps 2.1 and 3.1 classify each slit endpoint and external full boundary; step 7.1 uses bounded H3 boundary-node evaluation.
Step 2.2 constructs actual field by CC finite transversality; finite covers and triangles are supplied or explicitly constructed.

boundaries.reason: This is an actual disk index theorem, not an equivalence.
No existence of the disk or converse class characterization is asserted.
